summary: This new law sets out how the state can take back money and property gained through crime, as well as property used to commit crimes. Property can be confiscated after a criminal conviction and, in exceptional cases, without one. Before a case ends, courts can freeze property so it cannot be moved or sold. The bill also sets rules for managing and disposing of seized property, a fund for confiscated assets, and cooperation with foreign countries.
whyItMatters: People who profit from crimes such as corruption or drug trafficking could lose those gains even when a criminal conviction is not possible. Property owners and third parties need to know how freezes work and how they can challenge them.
keyProvisions: Confiscation of the proceeds of crime after a conviction (Chapter 5), using restraint (freezing) orders and confiscation orders, as listed in the table of contents.
In exceptional cases, confiscation without a criminal conviction, through civil restraint and civil forfeiture orders (Chapter 6).
Investigation powers including account monitoring orders and production orders (Chapter 4).
Courts may allow frozen property to be used for living and legal expenses (listed as a separate section under each freezing regime).
Rules for managing, storing and disposing of seized and confiscated property, and a fund for confiscated assets (Chapter 7).
International cooperation with foreign states, covering requests to and from other countries to freeze or confiscate property and sharing of recovered assets (Chapter 8).
whoIsAffected: People suspected or convicted of crimes, their families and business partners, banks and other holders of property, and law enforcement and prosecutors.
statedReasons: The government says the bill aims to stop offenders from benefiting from criminal proceeds by setting a legal framework to confiscate them, including without a conviction in exceptional cases, freeze them, manage and dispose of them, and cooperate with foreign states.
